rows.original:
Valkyrie is the title given to any person who has received Lumia's full blessing and been infused with her power. Lumia does not discriminate among races when giving her blessing, so it can sometimes be difficult to distinguish a valkyrie from another of their race. When exercising their power, however, the light of the sun glows in their eyes. Being that such a variety of races are taken in by the goddess of light, it can be hard to give an exact physical description. But regardless of race, Lumia's chosen tend to take on a motherly mien as they age.

        Lumia's blessing also bestows a certain level of femininity beyond mere androgyny. Even the strongest of valkyries have a supernatural softness to their features that belies the power beneath. Some valkyries find their breeder's aspects (whether it be the bust, hips, or genitalia) similarly enhanced. Regardless, the valkyrie shines with an inner vitality that marks her as one of Savarra's symbols of hope.
        
        A valkyrie's wings are also often a way to tell them apart from even the other winged races of Savarra. The wings can be feathered, in which case their feathers become speckled with flecks of metallic gold, or they can be formed of pure light, as if hewn from the sun's own rays. Regardless of what form they take, a valkyrie's wings grow to fit the perfect size for their bodies.
        
        To this day, the valkyries fight remnants of those very same Wraiths that tried to devour the known world. Their efforts lead them to the far corners of Savarra, and it's not uncommon to find valkyrie scouts working with Astrida salamanders to root out the corruptive influence of Wraith taint. Beyond the major population centers, however, it's rare to run into more than a few valkyries at once.
        
        Valkyrie efforts abroad aren't limited to only rooting out corruption. In addition to their combat endeavors, valkyries provide local populations with fertility blessings and other similar aid. They give smaller villages and hamlets a connection to the pantheon as a whole that is often otherwise completely unattainable.
rows.translation:
女武神”是指那些获得了卢米娅的全力祝福、并被注入了她力量的人。卢米娅在赐予祝福时并不会区分种族，因此有时很难将一位“女武神”与同种族的其他人区分开来。然而，在行使他们的力量时，他们的眼中会闪烁着太阳的光芒。由于这位光明女神接纳了如此多种族的生物，因此很难给出他们确切的外貌描述。但无论属于哪个种族，卢米娅挑选的这些生物在年龄增长后，往往会呈现出一种母性的气质。

        卢米娅的恩赐赋予了她们超越单纯中性的女性化程度。即便是最强大的女武神，她们的面容也带着超自然的柔美，这种柔美与她们隐藏的力量形成了鲜明的对比。有些女武神会发现，她们的生殖器部位也得到了类似的强化。无论如何，这些女武神都散发着内在的生命力，这使得她们成为了萨瓦拉象征希望的存在。
        
        女武神的翅膀也是区分她们与其他萨瓦拉地区的有翼种族的重要特征。这些翅膀有时由羽毛构成，此时羽毛上会点缀着金属般的金色斑点；而有时它们则完全由纯粹的光芒构成，仿佛是从太阳的光芒中切割出来的。无论采取何种形态，女武神的翅膀总是会呈现出与她们的身体完美匹配的大小。
        
        直到今天，这些女武神仍在与那些试图吞噬已知世界的怨灵残余势力进行战斗。她们的行动将她们带到了萨瓦拉的偏远地区，在那里，经常可以看到女武神侦察兵与阿斯特里达火蜥蜴一起努力，消除怨灵带来的腐蚀性影响。然而，在那些人口稀少的地区，同时遇到几名女武神的情况也是极为罕见的。
        
        女武神的海外行动并不仅限于打击腐败。除了参与战斗之外，她们还为当地居民提供生育祝福及其他类似的援助。对于那些偏远的小村庄来说，这些帮助使它们能够与整个神系建立联系，而这种联系在其他情况下往往是完全无法实现的。
rows.raw:
"
        Valkyrie is the title given to any person who has received Lumia's full blessing and been infused with her power. Lumia does not discriminate among races when giving her blessing, so it can sometimes be difficult to distinguish a valkyrie from another of their race. When exercising their power, however, the light of the sun glows in their eyes. Being that such a variety of races are taken in by the goddess of light, it can be hard to give an exact physical description. But regardless of race, Lumia's chosen tend to take on a motherly mien as they age.

        Lumia's blessing also bestows a certain level of femininity beyond mere androgyny. Even the strongest of valkyries have a supernatural softness to their features that belies the power beneath. Some valkyries find their breeder's aspects (whether it be the bust, hips, or genitalia) similarly enhanced. Regardless, the valkyrie shines with an inner vitality that marks her as one of Savarra's symbols of hope.
        
        A valkyrie's wings are also often a way to tell them apart from even the other winged races of Savarra. The wings can be feathered, in which case their feathers become speckled with flecks of metallic gold, or they can be formed of pure light, as if hewn from the sun's own rays. Regardless of what form they take, a valkyrie's wings grow to fit the perfect size for their bodies.
        
        To this day, the valkyries fight remnants of those very same Wraiths that tried to devour the known world. Their efforts lead them to the far corners of Savarra, and it's not uncommon to find valkyrie scouts working with Astrida salamanders to root out the corruptive influence of Wraith taint. Beyond the major population centers, however, it's rare to run into more than a few valkyries at once.
        
        Valkyrie efforts abroad aren't limited to only rooting out corruption. In addition to their combat endeavors, valkyries provide local populations with fertility blessings and other similar aid. They give smaller villages and hamlets a connection to the pantheon as a whole that is often otherwise completely unattainable. 

        "

rows.original:
Contrary to what one might expect from those chosen by the goddess of fertility, most valkyries choose to remain childless during their tenure. Instead, they assist others with pregnancy and childbirth in their stead. Retired valkyries often have children of their own, settling down with former wingmates or lovers met during their duties.
        
        Through a godly rite known as Effulgent Transference, Lumia is capable of moving a fertilized egg from one mother's womb to another. Among valkyries, the act of assisting an ailing or fragile mother and carrying her child to term is a great honor. The sun-blessed surrogate will often stay with the mother (and their partner if they have one), providing attention and sharing their experiences as the pregnancy progresses.
        
        When not stationed in a specific place, a valkyrie's duties are rarely imposed upon during this sacred duty. Many even continue to work during the daytime hours. Even the later stages of pregnancy tend to not hinder a valkyrie, with Lumia's blessings protecting the child in their wombs from harm.
rows.translation:
与人们可能想象的不同，那些被生育女神选中的女性们，大多数在担任这一职责期间选择不生育。相反，她们会帮助他人完成怀孕和分娩的过程。那些退休后的女武神们，往往也会自己生儿育女，与曾经并肩作战的战友或在执行任务期间相识的恋人一起安定下来生活。
        
        通过一种被称为“光辉转移”的神圣仪式，卢米娅能够将已经受精的胚胎从一位母亲的子宫转移到另一位母亲的子宫中。在女武神们看来，帮助那些身体虚弱或处于困境中的母亲，并帮助她们顺利生下孩子，是一项无比光荣的使命。这个受到阳光眷顾的代孕者通常会陪伴在母亲身边（如果她们有伴侣的话，也会与伴侣一起），在怀孕期间给予母亲关怀，并与她分享自己的经历。
        
        而当这位代孕者没有固定驻扎地点时，在履行这一神圣职责的过程中，她的其他任务也很少会被安排。许多人甚至在白天也会继续工作。即使是在怀孕的后期阶段，这也并不会妨碍这些女性继续履行她们的职责，因为卢米娅的庇护使得她们腹中的胎儿能够免受任何伤害。

rows.original:
Tales of Lumia facing down formless terrors and wicked monsters stretch back into infinity, but never her alone. Wherever tales of Lumia's exploits are found, so too are the stories of those whose souls she rescued from the clutch of oblivion. According to the legends, the original valkyries were created when a pilgrimage of Lumia's favored devotees were beset by a wicked, many-headed serpent. Unable to bear the sight of them on the cusp of death, the goddess of life swept in and granted them the strength to overcome their foe. 

        Rescued from death, these first valkyries joined Lumia in her travels throughout the world. While she focused on creation and the blessings of motherhood, the valkyries assisted her, ensuring her safety when she was vulnerable, and bringing news of what areas in the world needed a helping hand. 
        
        During the Godswar, more valkyries were made than during the entire existence of the world before it. Lumia fought side by side with pale elves, humans, lupines, kitsune, minotaurs, siorcana, salamanders, and every other race fighting to protect their livelihoods from the Wraiths. The sun goddess stormed through the battlefields, plucking meals from the very fangs of the Wraiths and restoring them to glorious splendor. 
        
        After the war, the valkyries returned to Lumia's palace, and have continued to assist her since then. New would-be valkyries take part in trials to determine the mettle of their souls and whether they're truly ready to join Lumia's service. Most modern members of the order come from the reclusive boreal elf capital of the Winter City, but anyone is welcome to make the pilgrimage.
rows.translation:
关于卢米娅的故事，讲述着她如何与无形的恐惧与邪恶的怪物抗争，这些故事仿佛延伸至无尽的远方，但绝不仅仅只有她一个人的故事。无论在哪里，只要能找到关于卢米娅英勇事迹的记载，就必然也会看到那些因为她的帮助而从遗忘的边缘被拯救出来的人们的故事。根据传说，最初的瓦尔基里们是在卢米娅的忠实信徒们在进行朝圣途中遭遇一条邪恶的多头巨蛇时被创造出来的。看到信徒们即将面临死亡，生命女神及时出现，赋予他们战胜敌人的力量。 

        从死亡中获救的这些女武神，随后加入了卢米娅的行列，陪伴她走遍世界各地。当卢米娅专注于创造与母性的喜悦时，这些女武神会守护她的安全，在她遇到危险时给予帮助，同时也会告知她世界上哪些地方需要援助。 
        
        在神战期间，被创造出来的女武神数量，超过了这个世界诞生以来所创造的所有女武神的总量。卢米娅与苍白精灵、人类、狼族、狐妖、弥诺陶洛斯、西奥卡娜族、火蜥蜴以及其他所有种族并肩作战，共同保卫自己的家园，抵御那些幽灵的侵袭。太阳女神穿梭在战场上，从那些幽灵的獠牙中夺回被吞噬的生命，让它们重新恢复往日的辉煌。 
        
        战争结束后，这些女武神们回到了卢米娅的宫殿，从那时起便一直陪伴在她身边。那些有志成为女武神的人需要通过一系列考验，来证明自己内心的勇气以及是否真的适合为卢米娅效力。这个组织中的现代成员大多来自那座与世隔绝的极北精灵之都——冬城，但任何人都可以前来参加这些选拔。

rows.original:
Being without a country or nation to call their own, valkyrie's have more of a camaraderie than a culture. Each valkyrie welcomes newcomers into the mix, and the great diversity of races between them leads to an understanding of culture that would otherwise be impossible. Valkyries adjusted to life in Lumias palace are often surprised to find townsfolk in the Marches skittish around kitsune, or even the valkyrie themselves. Their straightforward attitudes about such things can cause consternation.

        The valkyries abhor Lumia's name being used in the name of plunder and false ideology. Invaders seeking to "enlighten" civilized races to Lumia's faith by desecrating their lands and destroying their faiths can often find their tents and boats razed and sunk in flashes of radiant light. 
        
        The vast majority of valkyries live in Lumia's palace, but it's not uncommon to find them in other parts of the world. At least two valkyries are assigned to each of the world's major population centers at any given time, monitoring for traces of Wraithspawn and ensuring communication with the palace. Other valkyries are often assigned to protect Lumian devotees during their pregnancies, particularly royalty under threat of potential political assassination or jealous vengeance.
rows.translation:
由于没有属于自己的国家或民族，这些女武神们所拥有的更多是一种同志情谊，而非真正的文化传统。每一位女武神都会热情欢迎新成员的加入，而她们之间不同的种族背景使得她们能够理解各种不同的文化，这种理解在其他情况下是无法实现的。那些已经适应了在卢米亚斯宫殿生活的女武神们，常常会惊讶地发现，边境地区的镇民们对狐妖，甚至对女武神本身，都会表现出一种紧张和畏惧的态度。她们这种直率、坦诚的处事方式，往往会让人感到困惑和不安。

        女武神们憎恶人们将卢米娅的名字用来指代掠夺行为和虚假的意识形态。那些试图通过亵渎其他文明的领土、摧毁他们的信仰来“引导”他们信奉卢米娅信仰的入侵者，往往会在耀眼的光芒中看到自己的帐篷和船只被摧毁、被淹没。 
        
        绝大多数女武神都居住在卢米娅的宫殿中，但在世界的其他地方也能偶尔见到她们的身影。在任何时候，世界上每一个主要人口聚居地都会至少有两名女武神被派驻在那里，她们负责监视任何与“幽灵卵”相关的踪迹，并确保与宫殿保持联系。其他女武神通常会被指派在卢米安信徒怀孕期间保护他们，尤其是那些面临政治暗杀威胁或嫉妒报复的王室成员。

rows.original:
Much like kitsune and the Astrida to their respective gods, valkyries are the foremost extension of Lumia's will in the world. They strongly resist any effort to change their physical being against their will, and have a measure of resistance to mental change as well. Despite these similarities, valkyries are the least static of any godsworn. They are perfectly capable of changing minor details about themselves using alchemy or other magic.

        Valkyries eat food in the same way they did before they received their blessings, and derive full sustenance from it. In times of need, Lumia's chosen can survive through a divine connection to their goddess and each other. This connection allows them to sense fallen comrades in need of aid, and provide magical healing from a greater distance.
        
        Valkyries work their magic with radiant flashes of light. It is not uncommon for even simpler spells cast by more magically inclined valkyries to include a flare of color or a burst of sparkling illumination.

就像狐妖和阿斯特里达分别是她们所信仰的神的化身一样，女武神们也是卢米娅意志在世间最直接的体现。她们会强烈抗性任何违背她们意愿试图改变她们的外在形态的行为，同时对精神层面的改变也具有一定的抗性能力。尽管存在这些相似之处，但女武神们却是所有受神明庇佑的存在中最不拘一格的。她们完全有能力通过炼金术或其他魔法手段来改变自己身上的某些细微特征。

        女武神们进食的方式与获得神恩之前一样，她们从食物中获取所需的全部营养。在危难时刻，卢米娅的选中之人能够通过与他们所信仰的女神以及彼此之间的神圣联系来生存下去。这种联系使他们能够感知到那些需要帮助的同伴，并且能够在较远的距离上施展魔法进行治疗。

rows.original: Even if its world-spanning hegemony was utterly broken by the Godswar and its aftermath, Old Belhar still bequeathed a legacy to the Savarra of today. Certainly, its architecture and symbols retain some iconic power, especially in what remains of the Heartlands. The state cults of the Seven that it once fostered gave birth to the often elaborate liturgy and practice of modern religion. And its language has spread far and wide, even if it has since begun to diverge into different regional dialects. But by far, the most indelible mark Old Belhar made on society was — and remains — the little electrum coin, or "hawk". The peoples of Savarra knew coins before the arrival of Old Belhar, but they were of varying weights and compositions. This made it difficult to trade reliably; one had a hard time determining how pure the silver in a silver coin was, and whether it had been shaved (reducing the amount of material on a coin that appeared the same as any other). Rulers in a financial pinch could and did reduce the proportion of precious metals in a given coin, altering its density but making up for it by changing the amount of metal in the coin to keep its weight the same. But this would also lower its value, especially once ordinary people found out about it... even if the rulers decreed that the coin would trade for grain or some other commodity at a fixed price. Without constant, universally accepted compositions, coins had to be minutely examined to determine their "true" value, a process as time-consuming and frustrating as barter itself. This changed dramatically with the Belharan discovery that a certain alloy of electrum with specific proportions of gold and silver (with a few other trace metals mixed in) served as a remarkably effective conductor of magical energies, and in particular was perfect for alchemy. Since electrum on a specific standard now had value beyond the commodity prices of the metals themselves, the rulers of Belhar had a strong incentive to coin on that standard and stick to it, rather than altering the proportions of the metals in attempts to extract value. Even a slight deviation from the standard would result in an alchemically useless lump of metal. On the Belharan standard, coins might have different weights (and thus different values), but coins of the same mass would have the same weight, same proportions of metals, and therefore the same value. It helped that Old Belhar had access to ready sources of electrum, both artificial and natural, and that it had achieved a broad political hegemony: it could introduce this new coinage with relative ease and the coinage would be accepted. Belharan rulers paid their soldiers and bureaucrats with electrum coin, and thus continually fed new hawks into the economy as those people in turn paid for their own needs with electrum, and so on. This is not to say that Old Belhar fully monetized the economy overnight. The vast majority of the population continued to work on the land, and had little use for coin; much of their tax burden was taken in kind, rather in cash, and went directly to feed the Belharan armies. And the electrum coin's value was still somewhat too high to enable easy use by the urban poor or for small transactions, spawning a multiplicity of low-value copper coins that only somewhat replaced barter for transactions in city marketplaces and at fairs. Furthermore, although the electrum hawk did have a fixed amount of gold, silver, and so on within it, the relative scarcity of trade goods in different parts of the Empire (along with local cultural conventions) meant that a hawk would still trade at different extrinsic values in different places. One could buy more wheat in the Heartlands with a single hawk than one could in the relatively cereal-poor Marches, for example. Naturally, the state attempted to control these prices through various universalizing edicts, but these were almost impossible to enforce and thus rarely altered the reality of the market. Still, the new electrum coin had an immediate, positive effect on the Empire's power. It enabled the government to tax more efficiently, it made trade significantly easier by reducing transaction costs, and it made recruitment easier by giving soldiers a more reliable source of income. Furthermore, it served as important propaganda for the Empire. On the reverse, every coin was stamped with the Belharan hawk icon, the state's chosen motif; on the obverse, the Emperor or Empress of the day would place their own portrait, along with an inscription of their name, epithet, and title. Thus, for example, "Laodike (III), Bringer of Peace, Empress of the Belharans." These symbols and coin inscriptions were almost always the primary contact that most Belharans had with their state, serving as constant reminders of who was in charge and permeating local life with their iconography. Old Belharan coins still have the power to astound with their tiny but detailed artistic portrayals of the Empire's rulers. Some insist that these portraits' expressions even offer glimpses into those rulers' personalities... although these claims ultimately say more about the beholders than they do about the time-weathered faces of ancient Emperors. Indeed, coins wear out. An electrum hawk exchanged between different people will lose tiny amounts of its mass to the handling process alone, to say nothing of those hawks that are consumed entirely in alchemy. Thus, a further marker of Belharan power was its ability to tax and to otherwise buy back coins for remelting, reminting, and restriking, to ensure that as many hawks as possible circulated at the appropriate weight. Not all coins would make their way back into imperial hands, even without counting alchemy. Often, coins were hoarded, buried, and forgotten — or their owners were killed without revealing their secrets. And other coins simply never circulated that frequently. One person's coin purse might contain hawks with portraits of rulers whose reigns varied by centuries. As Old Belhar disintegrated, the hawk perversely remained viable. In fact, during the early years of the Godswar, more coins were minted than ever before, a sign of the desperate crisis that the Empire found itself in and its frantic need to raise (and pay for) more soldiers. Later, however, miners died or fled, Wraiths depopulated towns, and the throne gradually lost control. For those places that remained populated, Belharan mints (which were generally established in areas with ready supplies of mined electrum, gold, or silver anyway) served as ready centers of power in the absence of imperial authority. They continued to coin on the same standard, because coined electrum remained valuable for alchemical purposes; their dies even continued to bear the hawk in many cases. It was only the rulers and their titles who changed, as would-be potentates and tinpot dictators attempted to spread their word of their power through coins and coin-portraits. Sometimes, Belharan armies loyal to the center would manage to retake the mints, slay the would-be ruler, and overstrike their portraits with that of the Emperor du jour. (With so many written sources of the time having disappeared, many historical accounts — insofar as anybody can create them — rely on careful examination of coin-portraits, die-marks, proofs, and overstrikes.) Despite their efforts, the Empire faded away, as did its armies; its enemies continued to multiply. But the coins persisted. Instead of attempting to coin on a different standard and reduce its expenses, the Belharan Empire and its successor states continued to use the same alloy, driven by the ubiquity of alchemy and a fear of appearing weak. Devaluation appeared less dangerous than converting more and more obligations from in-cash to in-kind. The great state farms were parceled out and granted to local aristocrats, who were already rarely supported by the resource-strapped imperial government in their struggles against Wraiths and internal foes. To do otherwise was not an easy choice. Those warlords who attempted to coin on different standards with less gold and silver in order to make those precious metals go farther (and to avoid alienating their sources of revenue) often found that their coins were not accepted by their soldiers, or by the vendors they attempted to purchase from. Nowadays, many city-states maintain their own mints, and the newly-produced coins usually remain on the Belharan weight standard. For want of plentiful skilled labor, the old mines are much less productive than they once were, but overstrikes and remelted coins from pre-Godswar hoards keep the circulating numbers up reasonably well; after all, as princess-historian Angeliki Doukas once wrote, "people died, but their coins did not." In fact, prices in electrum for some goods are now higher than they were under Belhar for a variety of reasons. With that said, most transactions remain a matter for barter or copper coinage; although most merchants will accept hawks, they are mostly useful for trading with people from far away. Long-distance trade is more dangerous and costly than at any point during the Empire's rule, but the hawk, at least, allows caravans and ship captains to be assured of getting decent value in trade when they do reach their destination. And when they get there, they can be similarly assured that their customers will be happy to take electrum, since it is coined on generally the same standard (if not in the same quantity) from Kitsuhon to Jassira. In the Frost Marches of today, almost all electrum coins are proper hawks, coined on the Belharan standard. They bear an almost absurd multiplicity of portraits, both of Belharan rulers long dead and of the leaders of the region's towns and cities, like Khor'minos, Maidenbridge, and Tychris. The most successful of the Heartland's rulers — and thus those who coin the most — can also be found on the obverses of Marcher hawks. And rarest of all, coins depicting the proud elvenqueens of the fabled Winter City and bearing the Ridell river emblem on the reverse sometimes appear in Marcher shops and markets, presumably dating from the tentative armed peace that persisted in the Frostwood during the days of Old Belhar. Coin portraits and legends are of somewhat inconsistent quality, due to the difficulty of finding skilled crafters. Belharan coins were so expertly crafted and error-free that they must — according to modern mint masters — have been created partially through magic. This technique, if it ever existed, has been lost, so that most of the die-work is now a matter for crafting by hand. (There are rumors that some mints in Tronarii and the Winter City retain the ability to make magic coin-dies, and the quality of their work would seem to substantiate this, but if so, they jealously guard their secrets.) Workers who inscribe the legends in their dies can make comical mistakes, reversing the words in their ruler's title or running out of space to place all the letters; that these errors still make it into coined hawks is a clear sign of the lack of quality control that besets most post-Belharan societies. Most ordinary Marchers would not notice these mistakes. In fact, most ordinary Marchers wouldn't use hawks very much at all in their day-to-day lives. But for an adventurer whose horizons extend across the whole of the Marches, they are absolutely essential.
rows.translation: 尽管在“神战”及其后续事件中，古贝尔哈那种横跨整个世界的霸权彻底崩溃了，但它仍然为今天的萨瓦拉留下了宝贵的遗产。毫无疑问，它的建筑风格与象征符号依然具有重要的影响力，尤其是在那些仍保留着古贝尔哈遗迹的腹地。它曾经扶持的七大神圣信仰，孕育出了现代宗教中那些往往极为繁琐的仪式与实践。而这些宗教的语言也传播到了世界各地，尽管后来逐渐分化成了不同的地方方言。但古贝尔哈对社会留下的最深远的影响，无疑就是那种由金银混合制成的小硬币，也就是人们所说的“鹰币”。 在古贝尔哈到来之前，萨瓦拉地区的人民就已经知道硬币的存在了，但那些硬币的重量和成分各不相同。这使得交易变得难以进行；人们很难判断银币中银的纯度，也不清楚这些银币是否被故意削减了重量（即银币的材质含量是否被减少了，而外观却与普通的银币没有任何区别）。手头拮据的统治者确实会降低硬币中的贵金属比例，从而改变其密度，再调整硬币中金属的用量以维持相同重量。但这样一来，硬币的价值也会下降，尤其是当普通人了解到这一情况后……即使统治者规定这种硬币可以以固定的价格兑换谷物或其他商品，情况也不会有所改变。在没有固定且被普遍认可的鉴定标准的情况下，人们必须仔细检查每一枚硬币，才能确定它们的“真实”价值——这一过程与物物交换本身一样耗时且令人沮丧。 然而，贝尔哈兰人的发现彻底改变了这一状况：他们发现，某种含有特定比例的金银（以及少量其他微量元素）的合金，能够成为极其有效的魔法能量传导介质，尤其适合用于炼金术。只要电铬合金是按特定标准制成，其商品价值便会远远超过其中贵金属本身的价值，因此贝尔哈的统治者们有着强烈的动机去按照这一标准铸造货币并严格遵守它，而不是通过改变金属成分的比例来试图获取更多的价值。任何稍微偏离这一标准的做法，都会导致铸出的金属完全失去其作为货币的价值。 在贝尔哈的标准体系中，不同面值的货币可能会具有不同的重量（从而具有不同的价值），但相同面值的硬币，其重量与金属比例都完全一致，因此价值自然相同。古贝尔哈拥有丰富的电铸金属资源，这些资源既有人工制造的，也有天然的；此外，它还掌握了广泛的政治霸权，因此能够相对轻松地推行这种新的货币制度，而这种货币也会被人们所接受。贝尔哈兰的统治者用电铬币来支付士兵和官僚们的薪酬，这样一来，就有更多的人将电铬币投入到经济活动中；而这些获得电铬币的人又会用它们来满足自己的需求，如此循环往复。 这并不是说古老的贝尔哈兰经济体系是在一夜之间就完全实现了货币化的。绝大多数人口仍然在土地上劳作，对他们来说，硬币几乎没有什么用处；他们所承担的税款大多以实物形式征收，而非现金，而这些实物直接被用来供养贝尔哈兰的军队。此外，银币的价值仍然偏高，因此城市贫民或进行小额交易时很难使用它们，这就促使人们铸造了大量低价值的铜币，这些铜币才在一定程度上取代了以物易物的交易方式，被用于城市市场和市场交易中。 此外，尽管这种“电铬鹰币”确实含有固定数量的黄金、白银等贵金属，但由于帝国不同地区贸易物品的稀缺程度各不相同，再加上当地的文化习俗，因此这种“电铬鹰币”在不同地区的交易价格也会存在差异。不同商品的相对价值仍会因地区而异。例如，在粮食资源相对丰富的中心地带，用一枚鹰币就能购买到比在粮食较为匮乏的边境地区更多的小麦。当然，政府会试图通过各种普遍适用的法令来控制这些价格，但这些法令几乎根本无法得到有效执行，因此也几乎无法改变市场的实际状况。 尽管如此，这种新的电铬币立即对帝国的实力产生了积极影响。它使政府能够更高效地征税，通过降低交易成本显著促进了贸易的发展，同时也为士兵提供了更稳定的收入来源，从而使得招募新兵的工作变得更加容易。此外，这种硬币还起到了重要的宣传作用。硬币的背面印有贝尔哈兰鹰的图案，这是该国选定的象征符号；而正面则会印有当朝皇帝或女皇的肖像，以及他们的名字、头衔等文字。例如，“劳迪克三世：和平的使者，贝尔哈兰人的女皇。 这些符号和硬币上的铭文，几乎总是大多数贝尔哈兰人与他们的政权建立联系的主要方式，它们不断提醒人们谁才是真正的掌权者，同时这些图案也渗透到了当地人们的日常生活中。古老的贝尔哈兰硬币，尽管尺寸小巧，但其上对帝国统治者的细致描绘依然充满了艺术魅力，令人赞叹不已。有些人坚持认为，这些肖像中的表情甚至能够让我们窥见那些统治者的性格……不过，这些说法实际上更多地反映了观察者的主观看法，而非那些历经岁月考验的古代皇帝们的真实面貌。 的确，硬币会随着使用而磨损。那些在不同人之间流通的电铬币鹰币，仅仅因为被反复拿取、使用，其质量就会减少一点点，更不用说那些被用于炼金术的鹰币了。因此，贝尔哈兰帝国实力的另一个体现，就是它有能力对硬币征税，或者回购这些硬币进行重新熔炼、重新铸造，从而确保尽可能多的鹰币以正确的重量在市场上流通。并非所有硬币都会重新回到统治者的手中，更何况还要考虑到炼金术的影响。通常，这些硬币会被人们囤积起来、埋藏起来，然后被遗忘；或者它们的主人在死亡时也没有透露出这些硬币的秘密。而还有一些硬币，根本就没有被频繁地流通使用过。某个人的零钱包里可能装着一些硬币，而这些硬币上印着那些统治者们的肖像，他们的统治时期跨度长达几个世纪。 随着旧贝拉尔的解体，这种鹰却出人意料地依然存活了下来。事实上，在神战初期，铸造的硬币数量比以往任何时候都要多——这恰恰反映了帝国当时所处的危急境地，以及它迫切需要招募更多士兵并为此支付巨额费用。然而，后来矿工们要么死亡，要么逃离，幽灵们使得许多城镇变得荒无人烟，王座也逐渐失去了对这些地区的控制。在那些仍有居民居住的地方，贝尔哈兰铸造厂——这些铸造厂通常建在那些拥有丰富电金、黄金或白银资源的地区——在帝国权威缺失的情况下，成为了当地的权力中心。他们继续按照同样的标准铸造硬币，因为这种由银和铜混合而成的合金在炼金术中仍然具有很高的价值；在许多情况下，他们的铸币模具上甚至仍然刻着鹰的图案。唯一发生变化的，是那些试图通过硬币和硬币上的肖像来彰显自己权力的统治者以及他们的头衔罢了。那些野心勃勃的权贵和那些自命不凡的独裁者，都在努力利用硬币来传播自己的权威。有时，那些忠于中央政权的贝尔哈兰军队会成功夺回造币厂，杀死那些企图称王的人，并在硬币上将当权皇帝的肖像刻上去取代原有的图案。（由于当时许多书面资料已经遗失，因此许多历史记载——至少在目前人们能够依据的那些记载中——都是通过仔细研究硬币上的肖像、铸币模具的痕迹、试样以及被修改后的图案来进行的。）尽管他们付出了种种努力，帝国还是逐渐衰落了，其军队也土崩瓦解；而敌人的势力却持续壮大。然而，那些硬币依然存在。 贝尔哈兰帝国及其继任国家并没有试图采用不同的标准来降低开支，而是继续使用同一种合金。这种做法的背后，是炼金术的普遍应用，以及人们对于显得软弱怯懦的恐惧。相比之下，货币贬值似乎比将越来越多的债务从现金形式转变为实物形式要危险得多。那些庞大的国营农场被分割出来，分给了当地的贵族们。而那些贵族们在与“幽灵”势力以及内部敌对势力的斗争中，本来就很少能得到资源匮乏的帝国的支持。因此，别无选择，只能这样做。那些试图通过使用较少的金银来制造标准不同的货币，从而让这些贵金属发挥更大的作用（同时避免得罪自己的收入来源），这些军阀们往往会发现，他们的货币既不能被士兵接受，也不能被他们试图购买物品的商贩们接受。 如今，许多城邦都保留着自己的铸币厂，新铸造的硬币通常仍然遵循贝尔哈兰的重量标准。由于缺乏熟练的劳动力，那些古老的矿场如今的产量已经大不如前了，但通过过度开采以及将神战之前的旧硬币重新熔炼，市场上流通的硬币数量仍然得以保持在一个相对稳定的水平。毕竟，正如那位公主出身的历史学家安杰利基·杜卡斯曾经所说：“人们可能会死去，但他们的硬币却会继续流传下去。事实上，由于种种原因，事实上，由于种种原因，如今某些商品以电铬币计价的价格已经高于贝尔哈兰时代。 话虽如此，大多数交易仍然以物易物或使用铜币进行；虽然大多数商人也会接受鹰币，但这种货币主要用于与远方的人进行交易。与帝国统治时期相比，长途贸易如今变得更加危险且成本更高，但至少鹰币能让商队和船长们确信，在交易中能够获得合理的回报。——前提是他们真的能够抵达目的地。而当它们抵达那里时，可以肯定的是，它们的顾客也会乐于接受这种电铬币，因为无论是在基图洪还是贾西拉，这种电铬币都是按照大致相同的标准制造的（尽管制造的数量可能有所不同）。 在如今的冰霜边境地区，几乎所有的电铬币都是按照贝尔哈兰的标准铸造的。这些硬币上刻有数量众多的图案，既有早已逝去的贝尔哈兰统治者的肖像，也有该地区各个城镇的领袖画像，比如科尔米诺斯、梅登布里奇和提克里斯。在“心脏之地”的统治者中，那些最为成功的人——也就是那些铸造最多货币的人——他们的形象也会被刻在“行军之鹰”硬币的正面。而最为稀有的，则是那些描绘着传说中冬城那些高傲的精灵女王、背面印有里德尔河徽章的硬币；这些硬币偶尔会出现在行军的商摊和市场里，想必它们可以追溯到古贝尔哈时代，当时弗罗斯特伍德地区还保持着那种脆弱的武装和平状态。 由于难以找到技艺高超的工匠，这些硬币上的肖像与传说图案的质量参差不齐。而贝尔哈兰的硬币制作得如此精良，毫无瑕疵，根据现代铸币大师的观点，这些硬币的制造过程肯定在一定程度上运用了魔法。如果这种技术真的存在过的话，如今也已经失传了，因此目前大多数铸币工作都只能依靠手工来完成。有传言称，特洛纳里和冬城的一些铸币厂仍然掌握制造魔法铸币模具的技术，而且他们的工艺质量似乎也证明了这一点，但如果是这样的话，这些工厂一定会严守自己的秘密。那些在模具上刻写这些铭文的工人经常会犯一些可笑的错误——比如把统治者头衔中的词语顺序弄反，或者因为空间不足而无法将所有的字母都刻上去。而这些错误最终仍然被刻在了硬币上，这一事实清楚地说明了：在贝尔哈兰之战之后的社会中，质量控制机制几乎已经荡然无存。 大多数普通边境居民根本不会注意到这些错误。事实上，大多数普通行者在日常生活中根本不怎么使用鹰币。但对于那些足迹遍及整个边境地区的冒险者来说，鹰币却绝对必不可少。
rows.raw: " Even if its world-spanning hegemony was utterly broken by the Godswar and its aftermath, Old Belhar still bequeathed a legacy to the Savarra of today. Certainly, its architecture and symbols retain some iconic power, especially in what remains of the Heartlands. The state cults of the Seven that it once fostered gave birth to the often elaborate liturgy and practice of modern religion. And its language has spread far and wide, even if it has since begun to diverge into different regional dialects. But by far, the most indelible mark Old Belhar made on society was — and remains — the little electrum coin, or "hawk". The peoples of Savarra knew coins before the arrival of Old Belhar, but they were of varying weights and compositions. This made it difficult to trade reliably; one had a hard time determining how pure the silver in a silver coin was, and whether it had been shaved (reducing the amount of material on a coin that appeared the same as any other). Rulers in a financial pinch could and did reduce the proportion of precious metals in a given coin, altering its density but making up for it by changing the amount of metal in the coin to keep its weight the same. But this would also lower its value, especially once ordinary people found out about it... even if the rulers decreed that the coin would trade for grain or some other commodity at a fixed price. Without constant, universally accepted compositions, coins had to be minutely examined to determine their "true" value, a process as time-consuming and frustrating as barter itself. This changed dramatically with the Belharan discovery that a certain alloy of electrum with specific proportions of gold and silver (with a few other trace metals mixed in) served as a remarkably effective conductor of magical energies, and in particular was perfect for alchemy. Since electrum on a specific standard now had value beyond the commodity prices of the metals themselves, the rulers of Belhar had a strong incentive to coin on that standard and stick to it, rather than altering the proportions of the metals in attempts to extract value. Even a slight deviation from the standard would result in an alchemically useless lump of metal. On the Belharan standard, coins might have different weights (and thus different values), but coins of the same mass would have the same weight, same proportions of metals, and therefore the same value. It helped that Old Belhar had access to ready sources of electrum, both artificial and natural, and that it had achieved a broad political hegemony: it could introduce this new coinage with relative ease and the coinage would be accepted. Belharan rulers paid their soldiers and bureaucrats with electrum coin, and thus continually fed new hawks into the economy as those people in turn paid for their own needs with electrum, and so on. This is not to say that Old Belhar fully monetized the economy overnight. The vast majority of the population continued to work on the land, and had little use for coin; much of their tax burden was taken in kind, rather in cash, and went directly to feed the Belharan armies. And the electrum coin's value was still somewhat too high to enable easy use by the urban poor or for small transactions, spawning a multiplicity of low-value copper coins that only somewhat replaced barter for transactions in city marketplaces and at fairs. Furthermore, although the electrum hawk did have a fixed amount of gold, silver, and so on within it, the relative scarcity of trade goods in different parts of the Empire (along with local cultural conventions) meant that a hawk would still trade at different extrinsic values in different places. One could buy more wheat in the Heartlands with a single hawk than one could in the relatively cereal-poor Marches, for example. Naturally, the state attempted to control these prices through various universalizing edicts, but these were almost impossible to enforce and thus rarely altered the reality of the market. Still, the new electrum coin had an immediate, positive effect on the Empire's power. It enabled the government to tax more efficiently, it made trade significantly easier by reducing transaction costs, and it made recruitment easier by giving soldiers a more reliable source of income. Furthermore, it served as important propaganda for the Empire. On the reverse, every coin was stamped with the Belharan hawk icon, the state's chosen motif; on the obverse, the Emperor or Empress of the day would place their own portrait, along with an inscription of their name, epithet, and title. Thus, for example, "Laodike (III), Bringer of Peace, Empress of the Belharans." These symbols and coin inscriptions were almost always the primary contact that most Belharans had with their state, serving as constant reminders of who was in charge and permeating local life with their iconography. Old Belharan coins still have the power to astound with their tiny but detailed artistic portrayals of the Empire's rulers. Some insist that these portraits' expressions even offer glimpses into those rulers' personalities... although these claims ultimately say more about the beholders than they do about the time-weathered faces of ancient Emperors. Indeed, coins wear out. An electrum hawk exchanged between different people will lose tiny amounts of its mass to the handling process alone, to say nothing of those hawks that are consumed entirely in alchemy. Thus, a further marker of Belharan power was its ability to tax and to otherwise buy back coins for remelting, reminting, and restriking, to ensure that as many hawks as possible circulated at the appropriate weight. Not all coins would make their way back into imperial hands, even without counting alchemy. Often, coins were hoarded, buried, and forgotten — or their owners were killed without revealing their secrets. And other coins simply never circulated that frequently. One person's coin purse might contain hawks with portraits of rulers whose reigns varied by centuries. As Old Belhar disintegrated, the hawk perversely remained viable. In fact, during the early years of the Godswar, more coins were minted than ever before, a sign of the desperate crisis that the Empire found itself in and its frantic need to raise (and pay for) more soldiers. Later, however, miners died or fled, Wraiths depopulated towns, and the throne gradually lost control. For those places that remained populated, Belharan mints (which were generally established in areas with ready supplies of mined electrum, gold, or silver anyway) served as ready centers of power in the absence of imperial authority. They continued to coin on the same standard, because coined electrum remained valuable for alchemical purposes; their dies even continued to bear the hawk in many cases. It was only the rulers and their titles who changed, as would-be potentates and tinpot dictators attempted to spread their word of their power through coins and coin-portraits. Sometimes, Belharan armies loyal to the center would manage to retake the mints, slay the would-be ruler, and overstrike their portraits with that of the Emperor du jour. (With so many written sources of the time having disappeared, many historical accounts — insofar as anybody can create them — rely on careful examination of coin-portraits, die-marks, proofs, and overstrikes.) Despite their efforts, the Empire faded away, as did its armies; its enemies continued to multiply. But the coins persisted. Instead of attempting to coin on a different standard and reduce its expenses, the Belharan Empire and its successor states continued to use the same alloy, driven by the ubiquity of alchemy and a fear of appearing weak. Devaluation appeared less dangerous than converting more and more obligations from in-cash to in-kind. The great state farms were parceled out and granted to local aristocrats, who were already rarely supported by the resource-strapped imperial government in their struggles against Wraiths and internal foes. To do otherwise was not an easy choice. Those warlords who attempted to coin on different standards with less gold and silver in order to make those precious metals go farther (and to avoid alienating their sources of revenue) often found that their coins were not accepted by their soldiers, or by the vendors they attempted to purchase from. Nowadays, many city-states maintain their own mints, and the newly-produced coins usually remain on the Belharan weight standard. For want of plentiful skilled labor, the old mines are much less productive than they once were, but overstrikes and remelted coins from pre-Godswar hoards keep the circulating numbers up reasonably well; after all, as princess-historian Angeliki Doukas once wrote, "people died, but their coins did not." In fact, prices in electrum for some goods are now higher than they were under Belhar for a variety of reasons. With that said, most transactions remain a matter for barter or copper coinage; although most merchants will accept hawks, they are mostly useful for trading with people from far away. Long-distance trade is more dangerous and costly than at any point during the Empire's rule, but the hawk, at least, allows caravans and ship captains to be assured of getting decent value in trade when they do reach their destination. And when they get there, they can be similarly assured that their customers will be happy to take electrum, since it is coined on generally the same standard (if not in the same quantity) from Kitsuhon to Jassira. In the Frost Marches of today, almost all electrum coins are proper hawks, coined on the Belharan standard. They bear an almost absurd multiplicity of portraits, both of Belharan rulers long dead and of the leaders of the region's towns and cities, like Khor'minos, Maidenbridge, and Tychris. The most successful of the Heartland's rulers — and thus those who coin the most — can also be found on the obverses of Marcher hawks. And rarest of all, coins depicting the proud elvenqueens of the fabled Winter City and bearing the Ridell river emblem on the reverse sometimes appear in Marcher shops and markets, presumably dating from the tentative armed peace that persisted in the Frostwood during the days of Old Belhar. Coin portraits and legends are of somewhat inconsistent quality, due to the difficulty of finding skilled crafters. Belharan coins were so expertly crafted and error-free that they must — according to modern mint masters — have been created partially through magic. This technique, if it ever existed, has been lost, so that most of the die-work is now a matter for crafting by hand. (There are rumors that some mints in Tronarii and the Winter City retain the ability to make magic coin-dies, and the quality of their work would seem to substantiate this, but if so, they jealously guard their secrets.) Workers who inscribe the legends in their dies can make comical mistakes, reversing the words in their ruler's title or running out of space to place all the letters; that these errors still make it into coined hawks is a clear sign of the lack of quality control that besets most post-Belharan societies. Most ordinary Marchers would not notice these mistakes. In fact, most ordinary Marchers wouldn't use hawks very much at all in their day-to-day lives. But for an adventurer whose horizons extend across the whole of the Marches, they are absolutely essential. "

rows.original: From "The Power of the Mind Unleashed: Dreamwalking and other Arcana Esoterica" by Jarlessa Thyri Astrid Gunvaldsen With the rise of the Belharan Empire and its passionate support of Estelore and other collegia arcana, the weaving of spells has progressed from a little-understood hedgecraft passed down between generations in oral form to a well-researched and documented art. Magic has become as accessible a topic of study in the empire as its history or economics. But even the full breadth of Estelorean spellcraft does not, after all of my dogged research through their archives and extensive interviewing of that storied school's most brilliant scholars, account for nor offer explanation of the supernatural phenomenon I will present an account of in this tome. It is my belief that there is magic in the world even beyond spellcraft, little understood or even acknowledged, that has escaped the notice of the empire — or perhaps has been pushed aside in favor of the easily-defined powers of its magisters. Over my many years of both private occult study and adventures afield throughout the northern limits of my husband's homeland, I have experienced magics that defy Estelorean understanding. I have seen men hypnotized by a resonance from the deep beneath the waves, or driven mad by the chime of a bell; I have felt witches enter my mind with a glance, trading thoughts more easily than one might speak them aloud; I have seen a bird-man of the high mountains bind his living soul to a great statue and become immortalized within it. Having seen these events and many more, I have come to believe that these are not the work of spellcraft as Estelore defines it, but another force within the sphere of magic entirely. It is my hope within these pages to explain my findings. First, let us remind ourselves that the working of aetheric energy into spells is accomplished by ritual invocation, using crystal or gem foci and words of power handed down by the First Wyrms to repeatably and reliably reproduce magical effects. Such is the origin of the most minor arcane prestidigitations through the most destructive and desperate of the blood-rituals ever performed by the southern barbarians, that which sank the Yvennese fleet off the coast of Zhenna and whose toll of death needs no repeating. Second, I will call on the wise words (born of decades of painstaking research into the patterns of the sleeping mind) of Arch-Magister Sigismund the Blind: "There is great power in dreams, for the landscape of dreams is the domain of the gods." It has long been attested by priests of all faiths that it is through dreams that divinities commune with their worshippers and give guidance to the faithful; I assert that there are those mortals who are also able to tap into the power of the Dreamscape, and shape the waking world in much the same way as the lucid sleeper shapes dreams. The Dreamscape is born of sleeping minds, all mingling together in the crystalline domain of the gods beyond our own senses. One cannot study nor perceive the dreaming world while awake (see the excellent work of the inestimable Grand Magister Caedwynn, who perhaps in my children's lifetimes will make his long-expected breakthrough in inter-planar travel); however, all of us interact with it, shape it and are shaped by it, while asleep. Only very rare individuals, what I have come to call Dreamwalkers, are able to manipulate the Dreamscape consciously — and, I believe, some few have discovered ways in which to channel their dreaming manipulations into the real world in the same way that the gods worked miracles in the ancient days, or now speak to their followers. Perhaps it may sound heretical, but I assert that the Dreamwalkers have stolen magic from the gods. With a thought, they are able to bridge the gap between waking and dreaming mind, communicating and even influencing thoughts of others; the more powerful among them are able to cause physical manifestation of their power — to lift and move objects, or excite energy into flame or calm it to a dead chill — without the use of arcane invocations or even magical foci. A Dreamwalker need merely focus his will, and the world responds; such feats defy our understanding of spellcraft entirely. Perhaps, as Grand Magister Caedwynn theorizes, this is only possible in places where the fabric between worlds grows thin and tired (though if so, this would suggest that the divine Dreamscape is a traversable world much like our own, or those that exist through portals); this would explain why Dreamwalkers are so rare, encountered only in the furthest reaches of the uncivilized world. What I cannot yet theorize is why or how Dreamwalkers awaken to their power, nor the full extent of what is possible through their manipulations of reality. The Avanai at least believe their Dreamwalkers have uncovered the secret of immortality, while the frost giants of the north-beyond-north speak in their sagas of terrible creatures able to harness power similar to that of dreamers. I must continue to unspool the mysteries of the Dreamscape...
rows.translation: 摘自贾勒萨·蒂里·阿斯特里德·冈瓦尔德森所著的《释放心灵的力量：梦游与其他神秘奥秘》 随着贝尔哈兰帝国的崛起，以及它对埃斯托洛尔等地区的热情支持神秘学院魔法咒语的编织方式，已经从那种代代口耳相传、人们知之甚少的神秘技艺，发展成为一门经过深入研究、有详细记录的艺术形式。在这个帝国里，魔法已经成为了与历史或经济学一样，可以被人们系统研究的学科。然而，尽管我通过仔细研究他们的档案，并对那所著名学府中最杰出的学者们进行了广泛的采访，但即便掌握了埃斯特洛瑞安魔法体系的全部知识，也依然无法解释或说明我在本书中将要描述的这种超自然现象。我相信，这个世界上存在着超越法术的魔力，这些魔力尚未被人们充分理解或承认，也可能被帝国忽视了——或者，或许是因为那些魔法师们所掌握的、易于理解的力量，这些魔力反而被忽视了。 在我多年进行的私人神秘学研究，以及在我丈夫故乡北部地区进行的种种探险中，我经历过许多超乎埃斯特洛里亚人理解范围的魔法现象。我见过有人被海浪深处传来的某种共鸣催眠，也有人被钟声逼得发狂；我感觉到女巫们只需一瞥就能侵入我的思维，她们交流思想的速度，比人们用语言表达还要快；我还见过那些生活在高山上的鸟人，将他们的灵魂与巨大的雕像结合在一起，从而获得永生。在目睹了这些事件以及许多其他类似的现象之后，我开始相信，这些现象并非属于埃斯特尔洛所定义的魔法范畴，而是属于魔法领域中的另一种力量。我希望通过这些文字来解释我的发现。 首先，我们需要牢记：以太能量被转化为法术，是通过特定的仪式召唤来实现的。这些仪式会使用水晶或宝石作为能量汇聚装置，同时运用那些由最初的巨龙们传承下来的咒语，从而让魔法效果得以稳定且重复地产生。从最简单的奥术戏法，到那些南方野蛮人曾经施展过的最为残酷、最为绝望的血祭仪式——比如导致耶文舰队在泽纳海岸覆灭的那场仪式，其造成的死亡代价实在无需赘述——所有这些，都是这一机制的体现。 其次，我想引用大法师西吉斯蒙德·布兰德的至理名言——这些智慧都是他经过数十年对人类睡眠状态的研究才得出的：“梦境之中蕴含着巨大的力量，因为梦境的世界乃是神灵的领地。长期以来，各种信仰的祭司们都证实：正是通过梦境，神明才会与信徒们进行交流，并为他们指明方向。我坚信，也有一些凡人能够驾驭梦境的力量，从而以与清醒状态下做梦者相同的方式，塑造这个现实世界。 梦境是由沉睡中的心灵所孕育而成的，所有这些心灵在我们的感官无法触及的神圣领域中相互交融。在清醒的状态下，人们既无法研究也无法感知这个梦境世界（不妨参考那位无比伟大的大法师凯德温的杰出研究成果——或许在他的子孙后代有生之年内，他就能在星际旅行领域取得期待已久的突破）；然而，在我们入睡的时候，我们都在与这个梦境进行互动，塑造它，同时也被它所塑造。只有极少数特殊的人，我将其称为梦行者这些人能够有意识地操控梦境世界——而且，我相信，其中有些人已经找到了将这种梦境操控能力应用到现实世界中的方法。就如同古代的神明会创造奇迹，或者如今还会与他们的信徒交流一样。 或许这听起来有些异端邪说，但我坚称，那些“梦行者”从神明那里窃取了魔法。他们只需心念一动，就能跨越清醒状态与梦境状态之间的界限，与他人交流甚至影响他们的思想；其中实力更强者甚至能够将自己的力量具现化——无论是举起或移动物体，还是将能量激发成火焰，或是将其彻底冷却至冰点——而这一切都不需要使用任何复杂的咒语或魔法道具。梦行者只需集中自己的意志，世界便会作出相应的反应；这样的现象完全超出了我们对法术机制的理解范围。 或许，正如大法师凯德温所推测的那样，这种情况只可能发生在那些世界之间的屏障变得薄弱甚至消失的地方（不过如果真是这样，那就意味着神圣的梦境世界也是一个可以穿越的世界，就像我们的世界或是那些通过传送门存在的世界一样）；这也能够解释为什么那些能够穿越梦境的人如此稀少，他们只出现在那些尚未开化的边远地区。 目前我还无法解释，为什么或如何才能让“梦行者”觉醒并获得他们的力量，也不清楚他们通过操控现实能够做到什么。至少阿瓦奈人相信，他们的“梦行者”已经发现了永生的秘密；而那些生活在极北之地的霜巨人则在他们的传说中提到了一些可怕的生物，这些生物能够驾驭与“梦行者”相似的力量。 我必须继续揭开梦境之境的神秘面纱……

rows.original: "The Binding of the Lost," by Grand Magister Caedwynn of Estelore When a creature dies, most of its essence — what our priests would call its soul, or the primitive denizens of the eastern islands call ki — leaves the world as we know it. Some say the gods embrace the dead in eternity, while others contend that death is simply the end. The simple fact is: we don't know, because the dead don't come back. Not ever. What we do know is that when it passes, a creature temporarily leaves behind a shallow, fleeting echo of itself in our world: what we would call a spirit. The spirits of animals and most folk are impotent, without conscious thought or feeling, mere energy flowing through the aether before fully dissipating into the afterlife. At least, this is the natural progression of things; there are many tales both true (as investigated at length by your humble author) and mythical that describe the spirits of the dead becoming restless and refusing to move on from the mortal plane. These revenant spirits can be dangerous things, lashing out in anger or fear as they eternally relive the last moments experienced, and the emotions felt, by their true selves before death took them. Such spirits are so wrathful that they are capable of doing real physical harm to living things, manifesting themselves with just enough spiritual energy as to make claws and blades momentarily real when they strike. Do not be surprised, young mage, should you be called on to help your lessers to banish haunting spirits, whether real or imagined, from the land of our glorious and everlasting empire. It is your privilege and duty to turn your gifts to the defense of Belhar from threats supernatural. But for now, let us return our attention to the topic of this chapter: those fleeting spirits that are indeed content to slowly discorporate and become aetheric: Through ritual and spell, we magisters can summon these transient spirits, empower them to take semi-real form so that they can act or even communicate on our behalf. Many young mages learn to conjure the spirit of a wolf or some such creature to defend them against thieves and other miscreants. But such minor spirits are of little consequence to experienced magisters. What this volume aims to deal with are so-called "greater spirits," sometimes called Great Souls or Old Souls if you are of a mind to listen to elves on the matter. Creatures of great age and power, such as dragons, leave behind considerably more powerful — and, thus, more useful — spirits after death: spirits capable of unleashing tremendous power into the material world, given the magical spark to summon them. Such summonings are daunting tasks even for the greatest of our calling (such as your humble author), but through expert ritual and the assistance of arcane artifacts, summoning greater spirits is an art not beyond the reach of an experienced and well-educated magister. Now, the question most young pupils ask when confronted with this truth is "What can I do with one of these greater spirits?" The answer depends entirely on your mastery of your craft, young mage. Great spirits can be commanded to fight or otherwise act on your behalf, as their lesser cousins can, but we Estelorean magisters have in the last few decades uncovered a new science, one that greatly magnifies the potential of powerful spirits. We call it, simply, spirit binding. Spirit binding allows the mage to permanently seal a spirit of great power within an object of imperial quality, infusing the item with the spirit's very essence. The spirit of a flame-wreathed drake might give a blade a perpetual coating of flame, or proof a mage's robe or warrior's panoply against flame. The spirits of the greatest and most powerful of creatures can sometimes even retain a hint of their former selves: intelligence, even memories, given voice in their master's head. It makes one think about just how permanent death really is, doesn't it?
rows.translation: 《迷失者的束缚》，埃斯特洛尔大法师凯德温著 生物死亡时，其大部分本质——我们的祭司称之为灵魂，而东部群岛的原始居民称之为气——会离开我们所知的世界。有人说诸神会在永恒中接纳死者，也有人坚称死亡就是彻底的终结。事实很简单：我们无从知晓，因为死者绝不会归来。 我们确实知道的是，生物死去时，会在世间短暂留下一个浅薄而易逝的回响，也就是所谓的灵体。动物和大多数凡人的灵体没有力量，也没有意识或感情，只是流经以太、最终彻底消散并进入来世的能量。至少，事物本应如此发展；然而许多真实故事（经鄙人详尽调查）与神话都描述过躁动不安、拒绝离开凡世的死者灵体。这些亡魂可能十分危险：它们永远重演本体死前最后经历的时刻与情绪，因愤怒或恐惧而攻击旁人。它们的怨恨如此强烈，甚至能够真正伤害活物；攻击时，它们会凝聚足够的灵能，让利爪与刀刃在一瞬间化为实体。 年轻的法师，若有人请你帮助下等之人，将真实或臆想的作祟灵体逐出我们光荣而永恒的帝国领土，请勿感到惊讶。运用天赋保护贝尔哈免受超自然威胁，既是你的特权，也是你的责任。不过现在，让我们回到本章的主题：那些甘愿慢慢失去形体、化入以太的短暂灵体。 通过仪式和法术，我们法师可以召来这些转瞬即逝的灵体，赋予它们半实体形态，使其代我们行动，甚至与人交流。许多年轻法师都会学习召唤狼或类似生物的灵体，用以保护自己免受盗贼及其他恶徒侵害。 但对经验丰富的法师而言，这种弱小灵体无足轻重。本卷真正讨论的是所谓的“强大灵体”；若你愿意听信精灵的说法，也可称其为“伟大灵魂”或“古老灵魂”。巨龙等古老而强大的生物死后，会留下强大得多、因而也有用得多的灵体。只需用魔法火花将其召来，它们便能向物质世界释放惊人力量。即使对本行最伟大的人物（例如鄙人）而言，这类召唤也是艰巨挑战；不过，凭借精深仪式和奥术器物的协助，召唤强大灵体并非经验丰富、受过良好教育的法师无法企及的技艺。 面对这一事实，大多数年轻学生首先会问：“我能用这些强大灵体做什么？”答案完全取决于你对自身技艺的掌握，年轻的法师。强大灵体可以像弱小同类一样，受命替你战斗或执行其他行动；而近几十年来，我们埃斯特洛尔法师还发现了一门新学问，能极大提升强大灵体的潜力。我们简单地称之为灵体束缚。 灵体束缚能让法师把强大灵体永久封进帝国品质的器物，使器物浸透灵体本身的本质。周身缠绕火焰的龙兽之灵，可以让刀刃永远燃烧，也可以使法袍或战士甲胄免受烈火侵袭。最伟大、最强悍的生物之灵，有时甚至能保留些许生前的自我——智慧乃至记忆——并在主人的脑海中发出声音。 这不禁让人思考：死亡究竟有多么永久，不是吗？
rows.raw: " "The Binding of the Lost," by Grand Magister Caedwynn of Estelore When a creature dies, most of its essence — what our priests would call its soul, or the primitive denizens of the eastern islands call ki — leaves the world as we know it. Some say the gods embrace the dead in eternity, while others contend that death is simply the end. The simple fact is: we don't know, because the dead don't come back. Not ever. What we do know is that when it passes, a creature temporarily leaves behind a shallow, fleeting echo of itself in our world: what we would call a spirit. The spirits of animals and most folk are impotent, without conscious thought or feeling, mere energy flowing through the aether before fully dissipating into the afterlife. At least, this is the natural progression of things; there are many tales both true (as investigated at length by your humble author) and mythical that describe the spirits of the dead becoming restless and refusing to move on from the mortal plane. These revenant spirits can be dangerous things, lashing out in anger or fear as they eternally relive the last moments experienced, and the emotions felt, by their true selves before death took them. Such spirits are so wrathful that they are capable of doing real physical harm to living things, manifesting themselves with just enough spiritual energy as to make claws and blades momentarily real when they strike. Do not be surprised, young mage, should you be called on to help your lessers to banish haunting spirits, whether real or imagined, from the land of our glorious and everlasting empire. It is your privilege and duty to turn your gifts to the defense of Belhar from threats supernatural. But for now, let us return our attention to the topic of this chapter: those fleeting spirits that are indeed content to slowly discorporate and become aetheric: Through ritual and spell, we magisters can summon these transient spirits, empower them to take semi-real form so that they can act or even communicate on our behalf. Many young mages learn to conjure the spirit of a wolf or some such creature to defend them against thieves and other miscreants. But such minor spirits are of little consequence to experienced magisters. What this volume aims to deal with are so-called "greater spirits," sometimes called Great Souls or Old Souls if you are of a mind to listen to elves on the matter. Creatures of great age and power, such as dragons, leave behind considerably more powerful — and, thus, more useful — spirits after death: spirits capable of unleashing tremendous power into the material world, given the magical spark to summon them. Such summonings are daunting tasks even for the greatest of our calling (such as your humble author), but through expert ritual and the assistance of arcane artifacts, summoning greater spirits is an art not beyond the reach of an experienced and well-educated magister. Now, the question most young pupils ask when confronted with this truth is "What can I do with one of these greater spirits?" The answer depends entirely on your mastery of your craft, young mage. Great spirits can be commanded to fight or otherwise act on your behalf, as their lesser cousins can, but we Estelorean magisters have in the last few decades uncovered a new science, one that greatly magnifies the potential of powerful spirits. We call it, simply, spirit binding. Spirit binding allows the mage to permanently seal a spirit of great power within an object of imperial quality, infusing the item with the spirit's very essence. The spirit of a flame-wreathed drake might give a blade a perpetual coating of flame, or proof a mage's robe or warrior's panoply against flame. The spirits of the greatest and most powerful of creatures can sometimes even retain a hint of their former selves: intelligence, even memories, given voice in their master's head. It makes one think about just how permanent death really is, doesn't it?"

rows.original: Outside of a select few, formal education is largely unknown to Savarrans. No one knows exactly how widespread literacy is, but the best guesses place it at less than a tenth of the population. Knowledge of magic, while slightly more common, is largely confined to ordinary spells, with true mages and archmages a sadly (or beneficially, given unchecked magic's role in nearly causing the apocalypse) tiny minority. And alchemy is hit-or-miss, with some casual knowledge using local herbs relatively common but really in-depth understanding limited in the extreme. Few rulers provide for the education of their city-dwelling subjects, and if one resides in the countryside — as most Savarrans do — the likelihood of having anyone other than perhaps a local hedge mage or witch for a teacher is approximately nil. This state of affairs is partly because of how close to the edge of starvation many Savarrans live their lives. Subsistence agriculture, pastoralism, and fishing still dominate ordinary people's daily rhythms, leaving them without much leisure time fit for education. Even when the time to devote to learning is there, the resources rarely exist; the few people who purport to have formal education in the countryside are often malevolent, or charlatans, or both. And many of the others possess the knowledge of what letters look like and how they sound but no actual literacy as such. Several of the current fables in the rural parts of what used to be Old Belhar warn against accepting the kindness of ostensibly learned strangers, and one can easily see why, given the number of unscrupulous mages promising power only to lure their charges into being magical experiments instead. As such, what skills one can find outside city walls are usually passed down by apprenticeship, tribal shamans, or family, and those are usually the practical skills of spoken language, herbology, arithmetic, personal organization, and whatever one needs to do to keep the food coming in throughout the year. To be clear, there are often rich non-written traditions that boast a great deal of creativity. The Godswar might have wiped out much, but one thing that survived was the rhapsodic profession, which blesses every town and village with its melodies. From traveling bards who keep all their songs in their head to loud village festivals to stories told over the firepit, the people of rural Savarra know how to create art. And even if reading is uncommon outside the cities, it's still possible to find educated travelers who can enthrall villages by reading stories out loud to an audience much like the rhapsodes memorize and sing their tales. In this way, many of the most famous written traditions have made their way out into the countryside in varying forms. And this flows both ways, too, for some of the great epics began as stories sung out in the country that were eventually put to ink. The sophistication of Belharan oral tradition speaks to the endless originality of the people who live outside cities' walls — and to the favor of Mallach, prince of passion and art. But it also speaks to the extent to which formal education and literacy do not exist in the countryside. In the towns and cities that remain amid the wreckage of Old Belhar the situation is different, and there are more ways in which a person can be trained and educated like the imperials of old. Personal tutors are thicker on the ground and more likely to actually possess the skills they claim to have. Some of the ancient imperial colleges still exist as academies of higher learning for the training of mages and scholars. The religious institutions of the Seven still school their acolytes in reading, writing, and in whatever magic is practical for temple clergy and paladins. To be sure, these courses of study, especially the former two, are still routes that exist primarily for those of means, who can afford to allow a child to spend valuable work time on things that will only pay off later in life. It is theoretically possible for a poor city-dweller to achieve a certain amount of literacy... but possible and likely are not the same thing. Khor'minos, with its great wealth and engineering prowess, is the most obvious exception to the rule that education is for the few. With the Minoans' customary combination of civic virtue and competitiveness (and, of course, the realm's prosperity), cowgirl magistrates take it upon themselves to tax citizens — and only citizens, not other resident subjects — an additional percentage to finance a certain level of formal education, much as they do with village games and other community events. This literacy has a purpose, even in the rural villages, for Minoans use inscriptions and the written word for most of their public notices. Many boys get their letters and take them into the legion, where they're used for military orders and inventories; many girls (and a few boys) go even further with additional understanding of rhetoric, history, mathematics, and engineering. Literacy is also not solely an urban phenomenon in the Deeprealms. Khor'minos itself, with its multiple city lycea, is the most well-educated, but depending on the village (and the magistrate, and the village teacher) even a rural cowgirl can emerge from her education capable of organizing a tunnel excavation, brewing safe alchemical potions, or holding her own in a poetry competition. The word 'can' is important here, for Minoan education is not compulsory, and even for those who attend a citizens' lyceum, knowledge retention rates are not always what Khor'minos' long-suffering cowgirl teachers would like. Compared to most of the rest of what used to be the Empire, though, the Deeprealms are a veritable literary paradise. Basic literacy training, whether in Khor'minos or on the surface, generally involves the classics. The Belharan epics that survive, like the Tarandaiad and the Etymandrika, are common currency in both sung and written form, making them familiar objects for young readers. They keep listeners and readers interested with hefty doses of warfare, adventure, and romance, while also imparting moral lessons on how good and bad people behave. Advanced students develop the rhetorical skill to call upon these examples from the past for allusions. To be able to sing Euphrosyne's song or recite the grim warning of Demetrios[silly |, kyng of Inde, ] is to display one's learning and distinction on one's sleeve; to be able to replicate the meter of ancient Mallachite poetry is to lend your own work the same sort of gravitas. Learning by rote memorization is key here, establishing a vast library of details upon which one can call with relative ease. For those who continue on to even higher education, memorization remains crucial as one's repertoire of classics broadens. And spells — for the most rarefied levels of academia are always the arcane ones — are no different, relying on mental pathways and patterns of energy weaving that become much, much easier to follow for those who can turn them into over-learned behaviors through repetition. Even outside of Khor'minos, all this education is meant to be deeply practical; only the wealthiest of city nobility can afford to learn things without ever intending to actually use that knowledge. Those who learn to write do so because a business or ruler needs to be able to keep written records. Those who learn history do so at the behest of rulers who wish to buttress their claims to rule by creating politically useful narratives of their family's past, or to make a life singing the stories of the past for those with coin to spare, or to find Belharan ruins for the high-risk occupation of treasure hunting. Those who learn magic do so because their spells will help around the home, or protect them from harm, or slay their enemies. And rulers who maintain the old Belharan colleges do so because they expect a return on investment, often in the form of new or rediscovered potions or spells. They hold the power of the purse, which can make academia rather competitive. A scholar who can exceed her colleagues' accomplishments can become a legend, but one who fails to match them is usually out of a job in short order, consigned to village alchemy or attempting battle magic for bands of mercenaries. There is always a tension between the struggle to keep one's position and the shared community of learning and mentoring. Thankfully, collegiality still wins out most of the time... but not always. Magical institutions are subject to the vicissitudes of the southlands' endless wars, too. The riparian city of Marouka, for example, has managed to hold onto its ancient college, thanks to luck in warfare and a great deal of investment from the citizens' council. Marouka's warrior-scholars, urban militia, and riverine trade have ensured it a degree of prosperity amid the often-violent Belharan Heartlands, and would-be academics continue to flock to the city to try their luck at gaining grants from the council. Not all such cities have enjoyed the same sort of success, though. In days of yore, Marouka was connected to the college of Drapsa by
rows.translation: 除了少数例外，萨瓦兰人普遍不了解正规教育。没有人能准确知道识字率究竟有多高，但根据最乐观的估计，掌握读写能力的人口比例也不到总人口的十分之一。至于魔法知识，虽然稍微普及一些，但人们所掌握的也大多只是些基础法术；而真正的法师和大法师，却只是极少数人——这种状况既令人遗憾，也有些许积极意义，因为如果魔法不受约束，它很可能会引发世界末日。而炼金术则完全取决于运气和偶然性。虽然有些人会利用一些当地的草药进行简单的尝试，但真正深入研究这种学问的人却寥寥无几。很少有统治者会为居住在城市的子民提供教育机会；而对于那些生活在乡村的人——就像大多数萨瓦兰人一样——除了当地的草药师或女巫之外，几乎不可能有其他人能够担任他们的老师。 造成这种状况的部分原因在于，许多萨瓦兰人生活在几乎濒临饥饿的边缘。自给自足的农业、畜牧业和渔业仍然主导着普通人的日常生活，这使得他们几乎没有闲暇时间用于接受教育。即使有时间用于学习，所需的资源也往往难以获得；在农村地区，那些自称接受过正规教育的少数人，往往要么心怀不轨，要么就是骗子，或者两者皆是。而另外许多人，虽然知道字母的形状和发音，但实际上却并不具备相应的知识。读写能力正因如此，在那些曾经属于旧贝拉尔的乡村地区，目前流传的许多寓言都在告诫人们不要接受那些表面上博学高深的陌生人的善意。考虑到那些不择手段的法师们，他们总是承诺给予力量，但实际上却把受害者诱骗进去，让他们成为自己的魔法实验对象，这就很容易理解为什么会有这样的告诫了。因此，人们在城墙之外所能学到的技能，通常是通过拜师学习、部落萨满的传授，或是家族传承而获得的。这些技能往往包括口语表达能力、草药知识、算术能力、个人事务管理能力，以及那些为确保全年都有食物供应而必需掌握的实际技能。 需要明确的是，往往存在着一些丰富的非书面传统，这些传统蕴含着极高的创造力。虽然“神战”可能摧毁了许多东西，但有一样东西却幸存了下来——那就是那些充满激情的吟唱艺术。这些艺术为每一个城镇和村庄带来了美妙的旋律。从那些将所有歌曲都记在脑海中的游吟诗人，到热闹的乡村节日，再到围着火堆讲述的故事，萨瓦拉地区的乡村居民们深知如何创造艺术。即便在城市之外阅读并不普遍，仍然可以找到那些受过教育的旅行者，他们能够像那些擅长背诵和演唱故事的吟游诗人一样，为村民们大声朗读故事，从而吸引他们的注意力。这样一来，许多最著名的书面传统便以各种形式传播到了乡村地区。这种传播是双向的——一些伟大的史诗最初也是以口头故事的形式在乡村中流传，后来才被记录下来成为文字。贝拉汉口头传统的精湛程度，体现了那些生活在城市围墙之外的人们无穷的创造力——同时也彰显了激情与艺术之神马拉赫的庇护。然而，这一现象也暴露出一个事实：在乡村地区，正规的教育与识字率几乎不存在。 在那些仍矗立在旧贝拉尔废墟之中的城镇中，情况有所不同。在那里，人们有更多的途径接受训练与教育，从而能够像古代的帝国统治者那样成长。私人教师的数量也更为众多，而且他们很可能确实具备自己所宣称的那些能力。一些古老的皇家学院至今依然以高等学府的形式存在，继续培养法师和学者。七大宗教组织也依然教导他们的信徒阅读、写作，以及那些对神职人员与圣骑士来说实用的魔法知识。毫无疑问，这些学习课程，尤其是前两门，主要还是为那些经济条件较好的人准备的。他们有能力让孩子将宝贵的学习时间投入到那些只有在未来才能带来回报的事情上。从理论上讲，一个生活在贫困城市的居民是有可能达到一定的识字水平的……但“可能”与“很有可能”其实是两回事。 科尔米诺斯凭借其丰富的财富与卓越的工程技术，成为了“教育只为少数人享有”这一规则最明显的例外。由于米诺斯人向来将公民美德与竞争精神相结合（当然，也离不开这个王国的繁荣发展），那些身兼牛仔与法官双重身份的官员们便主动承担起了向公民征税的职责—— 只有公民，而非其他居民——政府会额外拨款，用于保障他们能够接受一定程度的正规教育，就像他们为乡村运动会及其他社区活动提供资金一样。这种识字能力是有其实际用途的，即使在农村地区也是如此，因为米诺斯人会在大多数公共公告中使用铭文和书面文字来进行交流。许多男孩收到这些信件后，会将它们带到军团中，这些信件被用于下达军事命令或进行物资清点；而许多女孩（以及少数男孩）则通过进一步学习修辞学、历史、数学和工程学，取得了更大的成就。 在《深境》中，识字能力也并非仅仅是城市才有的现象。拥有众多城市文理学院的科尔米诺斯，是受教育程度最高的地方；但即便是在乡村，只要接受了适当的教育——无论是通过村里的教师，还是当地的行政官员——即使是乡村的女牛仔，也能够掌握挖掘隧道、配制安全的炼金药剂，或者在诗歌比赛中展现出自己的实力。在这里，“可以”这个词非常重要，因为米诺斯的教育制度并非强制性的，即便是那些就读于公民文理学院的学生，他们的知识掌握程度也往往达不到科尔米诺斯那些耐心细致的女教师所期望的水平。然而，与帝国其他大部分地区相比，深境世界简直就是一片文学的乐园。 无论是在科尔米诺斯还是地表地区，基础读写能力的培养通常都会涉及经典文献。那些流传至今的贝拉兰史诗，就是这样的例子。塔兰代亚德以及Etymandrika这些内容以诗歌和散文的形式广泛流传，因此对于年轻读者来说非常熟悉。它们通过丰富的战争、冒险和浪漫故事吸引听众和读者的兴趣，同时也传达了关于善恶行为的道德教诲。对于水平较高的学生来说，他们能够运用这些历史典故来进行修辞表达。无论是吟唱欧弗洛辛的歌，还是背诵德米特里奥斯的警示语，这些内容都体现了这种能力。[silly |印度之王， ]这其实就是将所学的知识和才能展现出来；能够准确再现古代马拉克信徒诗歌的韵律，就能让自己的作品同样具备那种庄严与厚重感。在这里，死记硬背是关键，只有建立起庞大的知识库，才能在需要时从容地提取相关信息。对于那些继续接受更高层次教育的人来说，随着他们掌握的经典知识越来越多，记忆能力仍然至关重要。而法术——尤其是在学术研究的最高层次上——也不例外。这些法术依赖于特定的思维路径和能量流动模式，而对于那些通过反复练习将这些模式内化为习惯的人来说，掌握这些法术就会变得容易得多。 即使在科尔米诺斯之外，所有这些教育措施也都是为了达到深远的目的。实用只有那些城中最富有的贵族才有能力学习那些他们实际上从未打算使用的知识。那些学习写字的人，也是因为商家或统治者需要能够保存书面记录才这样做的。那些学习历史的人，其实是应统治者的要求这么做的。这些统治者希望通过编造与自己家族历史相关的、具有政治意义的故事来巩固自己的统治地位；或者为那些有钱人提供讲述过去的故事作为谋生手段；又或者为了寻找贝尔哈兰的遗迹，从而从事充满风险的寻宝活动。那些学习魔法的人，之所以这么做，是因为他们的法术能够帮助日常家务，或者保护他们免受伤害，又或者帮助他们消灭敌人。而那些维护着古老的贝尔哈兰学院的统治者们，之所以这么做，是因为他们期望从中获得回报——这种回报往往表现为新发现的药剂或法术。他们掌握着经济资源，这使得学术界充满了竞争。那些能够超越同事成就的学者可能会成为传奇人物，而那些无法达到这一标准的学者通常会很快失去工作，要么去从事乡村的炼金术，要么去为雇佣军队伍尝试施展战斗魔法。在努力维持自身地位与参与共同的学习与指导活动之间，始终存在着一种矛盾。幸运的是，大多数情况下，同事间的团结与合作仍然会占据上风……但也不总是如此。 魔法学院也同样深受南方地区无休止的战争所带来的影响。例如，位于河岸边的马鲁卡城，就因为在战争中运气较好，再加上市民委员会投入了大量资金，才得以保留其古老的学院。在贝尔哈兰内陆地区这个常常充满暴力的地方，马鲁卡的武士学者、城市民兵组织以及沿河贸易活动使得这座城市得以保持一定的繁荣。因此，许多有志于从事学术研究的人不断涌向这座城市，希望能够获得委员会的资助。然而，并非所有这样的城市都取得了同样的成功。在过去的岁月里，马鲁卡与德拉普萨学院之间存在着某种联系
rows.raw: " Outside of a select few, formal education is largely unknown to Savarrans. No one knows exactly how widespread literacy is, but the best guesses place it at less than a tenth of the population. Knowledge of magic, while slightly more common, is largely confined to ordinary spells, with true mages and archmages a sadly (or beneficially, given unchecked magic's role in nearly causing the apocalypse) tiny minority. And alchemy is hit-or-miss, with some casual knowledge using local herbs relatively common but really in-depth understanding limited in the extreme. Few rulers provide for the education of their city-dwelling subjects, and if one resides in the countryside — as most Savarrans do — the likelihood of having anyone other than perhaps a local hedge mage or witch for a teacher is approximately nil. This state of affairs is partly because of how close to the edge of starvation many Savarrans live their lives. Subsistence agriculture, pastoralism, and fishing still dominate ordinary people's daily rhythms, leaving them without much leisure time fit for education. Even when the time to devote to learning is there, the resources rarely exist; the few people who purport to have formal education in the countryside are often malevolent, or charlatans, or both. And many of the others possess the knowledge of what letters look like and how they sound but no actual literacy as such. Several of the current fables in the rural parts of what used to be Old Belhar warn against accepting the kindness of ostensibly learned strangers, and one can easily see why, given the number of unscrupulous mages promising power only to lure their charges into being magical experiments instead. As such, what skills one can find outside city walls are usually passed down by apprenticeship, tribal shamans, or family, and those are usually the practical skills of spoken language, herbology, arithmetic, personal organization, and whatever one needs to do to keep the food coming in throughout the year. To be clear, there are often rich non-written traditions that boast a great deal of creativity. The Godswar might have wiped out much, but one thing that survived was the rhapsodic profession, which blesses every town and village with its melodies. From traveling bards who keep all their songs in their head to loud village festivals to stories told over the firepit, the people of rural Savarra know how to create art. And even if reading is uncommon outside the cities, it's still possible to find educated travelers who can enthrall villages by reading stories out loud to an audience much like the rhapsodes memorize and sing their tales. In this way, many of the most famous written traditions have made their way out into the countryside in varying forms. And this flows both ways, too, for some of the great epics began as stories sung out in the country that were eventually put to ink. The sophistication of Belharan oral tradition speaks to the endless originality of the people who live outside cities' walls — and to the favor of Mallach, prince of passion and art. But it also speaks to the extent to which formal education and literacy do not exist in the countryside. In the towns and cities that remain amid the wreckage of Old Belhar the situation is different, and there are more ways in which a person can be trained and educated like the imperials of old. Personal tutors are thicker on the ground and more likely to actually possess the skills they claim to have. Some of the ancient imperial colleges still exist as academies of higher learning for the training of mages and scholars. The religious institutions of the Seven still school their acolytes in reading, writing, and in whatever magic is practical for temple clergy and paladins. To be sure, these courses of study, especially the former two, are still routes that exist primarily for those of means, who can afford to allow a child to spend valuable work time on things that will only pay off later in life. It is theoretically possible for a poor city-dweller to achieve a certain amount of literacy... but possible and likely are not the same thing. Khor'minos, with its great wealth and engineering prowess, is the most obvious exception to the rule that education is for the few. With the Minoans' customary combination of civic virtue and competitiveness (and, of course, the realm's prosperity), cowgirl magistrates take it upon themselves to tax citizens — and only citizens, not other resident subjects — an additional percentage to finance a certain level of formal education, much as they do with village games and other community events. This literacy has a purpose, even in the rural villages, for Minoans use inscriptions and the written word for most of their public notices. Many boys get their letters and take them into the legion, where they're used for military orders and inventories; many girls (and a few boys) go even further with additional understanding of rhetoric, history, mathematics, and engineering. Literacy is also not solely an urban phenomenon in the Deeprealms. Khor'minos itself, with its multiple city lycea, is the most well-educated, but depending on the village (and the magistrate, and the village teacher) even a rural cowgirl can emerge from her education capable of organizing a tunnel excavation, brewing safe alchemical potions, or holding her own in a poetry competition. The word 'can' is important here, for Minoan education is not compulsory, and even for those who attend a citizens' lyceum, knowledge retention rates are not always what Khor'minos' long-suffering cowgirl teachers would like. Compared to most of the rest of what used to be the Empire, though, the Deeprealms are a veritable literary paradise. Basic literacy training, whether in Khor'minos or on the surface, generally involves the classics. The Belharan epics that survive, like the Tarandaiad and the Etymandrika, are common currency in both sung and written form, making them familiar objects for young readers. They keep listeners and readers interested with hefty doses of warfare, adventure, and romance, while also imparting moral lessons on how good and bad people behave. Advanced students develop the rhetorical skill to call upon these examples from the past for allusions. To be able to sing Euphrosyne's song or recite the grim warning of Demetrios[silly |, kyng of Inde, ] is to display one's learning and distinction on one's sleeve; to be able to replicate the meter of ancient Mallachite poetry is to lend your own work the same sort of gravitas. Learning by rote memorization is key here, establishing a vast library of details upon which one can call with relative ease. For those who continue on to even higher education, memorization remains crucial as one's repertoire of classics broadens. And spells — for the most rarefied levels of academia are always the arcane ones — are no different, relying on mental pathways and patterns of energy weaving that become much, much easier to follow for those who can turn them into over-learned behaviors through repetition. Even outside of Khor'minos, all this education is meant to be deeply practical; only the wealthiest of city nobility can afford to learn things without ever intending to actually use that knowledge. Those who learn to write do so because a business or ruler needs to be able to keep written records. Those who learn history do so at the behest of rulers who wish to buttress their claims to rule by creating politically useful narratives of their family's past, or to make a life singing the stories of the past for those with coin to spare, or to find Belharan ruins for the high-risk occupation of treasure hunting. Those who learn magic do so because their spells will help around the home, or protect them from harm, or slay their enemies. And rulers who maintain the old Belharan colleges do so because they expect a return on investment, often in the form of new or rediscovered potions or spells. They hold the power of the purse, which can make academia rather competitive. A scholar who can exceed her colleagues' accomplishments can become a legend, but one who fails to match them is usually out of a job in short order, consigned to village alchemy or attempting battle magic for bands of mercenaries. There is always a tension between the struggle to keep one's position and the shared community of learning and mentoring. Thankfully, collegiality still wins out most of the time... but not always. Magical institutions are subject to the vicissitudes of the southlands' endless wars, too. The riparian city of Marouka, for example, has managed to hold onto its ancient college, thanks to luck in warfare and a great deal of investment from the citizens' council. Marouka's warrior-scholars, urban militia, and riverine trade have ensured it a degree of prosperity amid the often-violent Belharan Heartlands, and would-be academics continue to flock to the city to try their luck at gaining grants from the council. Not all such cities have enjoyed the same sort of success, though. In days of yore, Marouka was connected to the college of Drapsa by "

rows.original:
, but neither the portal nor the Drapsacan college exists anymore. The former was annihilated in the Godswar, and the latter burned to the ground when the city was attacked by the infamous Khushkan Horde. What remains is a barely-populated ruin that is but a shadow of even its post-Godswar self. Institutions of higher learning can readily find support from warlords and princes. They can become targets just as easily.
        
        Foreign armies are not the only danger to rulers whose reach for magical power exceeds their grasp. Under most circumstances, the Order Astrida, Nareva's godservants, are welcome sights at institutions of higher learning. After all, the Belharan colleges are universally graced by statues and icons of the purveyor of knowledge and keeper of secrets, and many a young student betakes himself to the shrine of the naga goddess to beseech her blessing. Astrida themselves are assiduous students of lore and arcana, and even the most warlike among them can hold her own in a conversation with excited academics. But their visits become considerably less friendly on those rare occasions when a mage starts to poke at the all-too-thin boundary of the space between worlds; they're far from a murderous magical inquisition, but a mage's conversations with an Astrida about magic are a bit chillier if that Astrida has just finished rendering that mage's dangerous portal device harmless. Fortunately, peer pressure from fellow academics — and the reasonable fear of a second apocalypse — usually prevents even the least scrupulous of mages from continuing their research far enough to gain the attention of Nareva's finest.
        
        One cannot say that Savarra after the Godswar is obscurantist, despite the dangers of portal magic and the wary eyes of the Astrida. But education in general, to say nothing of arcane knowledge, remains available to all too few, and is likely to remain that way for the foreseeable future.
rows.translation:
，但那座传送门与德拉普萨学院如今都已不复存在。前者毁于神战，后者则在恶名昭彰的库什坎部族袭击城市时被付之一炬。那里如今只剩一片人烟稀少的废墟，甚至连神战后的残破模样都不如。高等学府很容易获得军阀与王公的支持，也同样容易成为袭击目标。
        
        对那些妄图攫取超出自身掌控范围的魔法力量的统治者而言，外国军队并非唯一威胁。大多数时候，奈瑞瓦的神仆阿斯特里达教团都很受高等学府欢迎。毕竟，贝尔哈兰各学院无不供奉知识赐予者与秘密守护者的雕像与圣像，许多年轻学生也会前往这位娜迦女神的神龛祈求赐福。阿斯特里达成员本身也是勤勉的典籍与奥术学者，即便其中最好战者，也能与兴奋的学者侃侃而谈。然而，当法师开始触碰世界之间那层过于薄弱的界限时，她们少有的造访就不再那么友善。她们绝非嗜杀的魔法审判庭，但若一名阿斯特里达刚刚让某位法师危险的传送装置彻底失效，她与那位法师讨论魔法时，气氛难免会冷上几分。所幸，同僚学者的压力——以及对第二场末日灾难的合理恐惧——通常足以阻止哪怕最无底线的法师把研究推进到引起奈瑞瓦精锐注意的地步。
        
        尽管传送魔法危机四伏，阿斯特里达教团也始终警惕，却不能说神战后的萨瓦拉奉行蒙昧主义。然而，一般教育尚且只有极少数人能够获得，奥术知识就更不必说；在可预见的未来，情况恐怕仍会如此。
